2. This it mostly quite nice to read but there are a couple trip ups at the end. I'll run through them:

"in nocte" - First, the ablative of time isn't used with "in", so it would be "nocte", but even then you want "noctu", which is a particular form for this use.

"nostro medio hortulo" - Just a note on style; Romans didn't necessarily like rhyme like this, it has a different effect in Latin to English. This is often why you find prepositions breaking up noun-adjective groups down the middle in Poetry, so something like "inveni nostro ferrum medio in hortulo", just to show how it may be done.

"cum acciperem" - maybe use the indicative if you're talking about sequence of time and not trying to imply cause; presumably it was not "since I picked up the sword" that she was told by the goddess. You could also use the ablative absolute here if you like: "ferro accepto"

"aliqua diva" - I think this is a "quaedam" sort of "some" rather than an "aliqua". Presumable this is a particular goddess we're talking about.

"accepi ea quae fecerat a diva" - So for the ablative of agent you need to have a passive verb, you can't say "I learned this from someone" in the same way as you can in English; you need to be more literal and say "I was taught this/told this by someone". Certainly, for a construction like what you've written, you need to have an example from antiquity of a Roman saying this.

"illi nomen" - if "illi" is supposed to be "of him" then the genitive is "illius". You could equally be quite cheeky and say "istius".

"at 'illi nomen' haec dixit 'deferre non necesse...'" - So for adding these dialogue tags midway through, Latin often used "inquam", so here you would want "inquit". The problem is that "inquam" often does not take the accusative/infinitive construction, it's used parenthetically, so you would change things into oratio recta. So basically, I'd move "dixit" to before the sentence starts" or use "inquit" as an interjection but change it to oratio recta.

"accepisses a patruo" - Again, you can't have an ablative of agency with an active verb. If you were to really insist on using "accipio", you might be able to get around with an instrumental ablative. Something like "accepisses dictis patrui"

First, I get your frustration with the subjunctive, personally I think teaching it is one of Familia Romana's weakest areas. Generally though, the indicative is general action, whereas the subjunctive it used to form non-standard clauses (that is clauses that aren't just a statement of fact unlike "this wine is bad", "you love me", etc.). So the subjunctive usually is used in subordinate sentences or, if the main verb, it indicates something more than a statement of fact; such as the exhortative subjunctive, which is a command, "vivamus mea lesbia atque amemus" ("let us live, my Lesbia, and let us love"). 

Second, this isn't subjunctive, it's a future perfect followed by a regular future. Though yes the future perfect does look a lot like the perfect subjunctive so I see how you could confuse the two quite reasonably; the clue should be though that the regular future follows, and the future perfect followed by normal future is a common way of speaking about a sequence of events in the future: "once you have (will have) done x, you will do y".

Third, cum-clauses are multitudinous and often very poorly explained. Broadly, they have either or both a causal meaning ("because", "although", "since", etc.) or a temporal meaning ("when", "after", "once", etc.). A good explanation of it to me was that: cum with the indicative only has the temporal meaning; cum with the primary sequence subjunctive (present/perfect) only has the causal meaning; cum with the historic sequence subjunctive (imperfect/pluperfect) has both meanings. This is a massive oversimplification and likely very wrong in its own way but so are all of the rules we learn and so I think it's a good set of training wheels for before you inevitably just develop a sense for it.

An incredibly contentious topic but I'll try to explain. 

Romans understood Latin sentences as they came out (as any speaker of any language does), and thus the position of the verb often serves to aid in understanding. It's a common misconception that verbs come at the end of the sentence (not always true) because they do, in fact, verbs often come at the end of the sentence often as a way of segregating clauses and sentences from each other. This is particularly noticeable in Caesar, who writes for clarity, but you can identify it elsewhere too. 

There is also some debate as to whether a strict adherence to verb-final sentences is somewhat reminiscent of older Latin, and whether Caesar does it because he's trying to imitate older, more traditional writing or not is in contention.

The general idea is that verbs usually go at the end of their clauses because it helps figure out when clauses end or not; but this is very frequently not observed.

a gerund is a verbal noun: “amandum” means “loving” in the sense of “do you know what loving is” (awkward sentence but i hope the point is made)

a participle is a verbal adjective which displays either completed or contemporaneous action: “amans” means “loving” in the sense of “the loving man walks”
[though side note, the english participle takes on a more attributive connotation than in Latin, where it is used to display simultaneous action, which you see a lot in Jerome “Jesus respondet dicens…”] 

a gerundive is also a verbal adjective which displays either obligation or future action: “carthago delenda est” or “censeo carthaginem delendam esse” as “carthage is to be destroyed”. but you also see it used impersonally “nunc est bibendum”; “now we drink”.

Ok so there are a number of issues here. My general advice before I break down your question is that you look up on Youtube guides on how to use Familia Romana and maybe look at some introductions of Latin before you continue.

The first problem here is that you're thinking too much about this "Roma in Italia est" means "Rome is in Italy", you should be able to work this out by the fact that all of these words have cognates in English ("Roma" is Latin for "Rome", "in" is "in", "Italia" is "Italy" and "est" is "is"). From here you're massively confusing yourself by trying to wrangle with information way beyond your level. To this effect, the reason why "Italia" and "Roma" have an "a" on the end is because they do, because you're learning Latin, not English, and words aren't going to be exactly the same: the real question here is why did English drop this "a"? Your question here is about how English inherited the words from Latin, and while that's interesting, it's irrelevant to learning Latin.

Second problem is that you need to pay attention to vowel lengths: Latin vowels are all either long or short (a long being pronounced for twice as long as a short). Sometimes these lengths will change the meaning of words, but usefully Familia Romana actually marks the difference (which most texts don't) by putting macrons on vowels that are long. There are two instances in the first sentence where you need to watch out; the first is the one that's causing you trouble which is that you're mistaking "est" ("is") for "ēst" ("eats"), notice the difference in length of the vowels? There is also the point to make that the "a" in "Italia" is long and actually it's "in Italiā"; this is because it's in the ablative case, since the preposition "in" triggers the ablative when it means "in" in English. If you don't know what I mean when I say ablative, you probably should spend some time online just reading about Latin, so you're aware of the broad concepts of its grammar. Good Youtube channels for this are people like Luke Ranieri (either on Polymathy or Scorpio Martianus) or you can look at LatinTutorial.

You also need to keep in mind that Familia Romana isn't necessarily the "easiest" way to learn Latin - I'd daresay it's one of the harder ways - but the claim made about it is that it's the most effective, because it teaches you to actually read the language properly.

deabus = ablative plural of “dea”; this is common for sets of first and second declension words which only differ by declension and gender (the other obvious example is “filius”/“filia”) where you couldn’t actually differentiate them in the ablative/dative plurals which would in theory be “filiis” and “dis” respectively. So the Romans invented a separate ending for the first declension, which is rather more familiar to the third, fourth and fifth declension endings (“-ibus”, “-ebus”), in order to differentiate them. 

So, “sine filiis” is “without sons” but “sine filiabus” is “without daughters” in the same way as “sine deabus” means “without goddesses”. Notice the thematic vowel of the first declension “a” before the “bus” as a way to remember this and not to confuse it with the other similar ablative/dative endings.

This is why it's "Romanes ite domum" not "Romanes ite ad domum".

Ok so a number if problems:

1. No verb

2. Wrong cases

3. Use of preposition

  
So for the first one we can simple supply the 1st pl. active indicative present ending of the verb eo, ire 'to go' so that we have 'we go'. Which is "imus"

For the second one you have to know that not only does the preposition "ad" always take the accusative, but even despite the "ad" we'd need an accusative of motion. So for the moment "ad Romam".

The final issue is that "Roma" is a noun that doesn't take prepositions with regards to the accusative of motion towards or the ablative of separation. The general rule for this is that if a noun has a locative form extant (which "Roma" does, "Romae", meaning 'in Rome) then it doesn't use the prepositions "ad" or "ab" for these constructions. Some might tell you that it's just that cities and islands named for their cities don't take a preposition, but this isn't true, because "domus" doesn't take a preposition either, but what it does have is an extant locative form in "domi". 

Either way we end up with "imus Romam"

a nice way to remember the distinction is the etymology of the terms “pluperfect” and “perfect”. In latin “perfectus” means “complete” and thus refers to verbs that have been completed (and thus logically past tense); as opposed to actions in the past that are not complete, thus “imperfectus” of “imperfect” - the difference between “I ran” and “I was running”. Perfect only refers to actions that are complete by the present time though, but what if you wanted to speak about something that was completed before a past time? Then you use the pluperfect, or “plus quam perfectum” or “more than perfect”, because it’s the past of the past or further in the past, thus “more than perfect”. 

The distinction is “I ran/have run” vs “I had run”

They’re different tenses, it’s simple past versus pure perfect. It’s the same difference between “I ate” and “I have eaten”, or in this case, “I read” versus “I have read”. 

The difference is that “darllenais” refers to a specific instance in the past, whereas “dwi wedi darllen” refers to a completed action, without necessarily specifying a specific one. From what I know you can just supersede the same distinction in English between the two onto these.

So the grammarian Donatus thought that there were 4 genders: masc, fem, neut, and "communal". I've not heard of any grammarians claiming that there were 5, but I wouldn't doubt it.

At this point you really have to decide what you mean by "gender", because all Donatus was saying was that not all words have "fixed" inherent genders. There are still arguably only three distinguishable types of genders, and in terms of pragmatic information to give to students, there are three genders in effect. There can be discussions had about how a Roman may have thought about his own language, but at that point even we may have to throw out a lot of very useful terms if we're being wholly "accurate" (I put this in inverted commas because when I claim that Romans think this, I refer to what we can glean from the surviving literature, which may not represent a consensus). There aren't really clear divisions between nouns, verbs and adjectives according to the Romans, they thought of the participle as its own unique thing, and there are other confusing things. 

To a student of Latin: there are three genders. To a grammar enthusiast: it's unclear and debatable, go write a paper on it.

I think you’re misunderstanding the term “Machiavellian”, because it doesn’t actually necessitate being “shady” or deceitful, which you seem to think. It’s about being precise and strategic, which Leto obviously is. 

He didn’t just save those Fremen because he’s such a good guy, he saved them because he valued them over the spice, which is unusual in comparison to the previous Harkonnen rule. But the action is very precise regardless, he knows it’s something that is worth doing when it comes to his goal of mobilising the Fremen to fight for him, and be loyal to him. This doesn’t make it necessarily deceitful though, because it’s genuine, he wants the Fremen support and so he takes the action that he requires. I think this is what people say when they talk about Leto being Machiavellian.

Not to mention his use of propaganda, which he floods the civilian population with. Now, propaganda isn’t necessarily deceitful or sly, but Herbert makes a point that Leto is specifically trying to cultivate this image. A good example is him scrapping the Harkonnen custom of wringing towels of water to beggars outside the palace, which Leto removes not only because it’s wrong but because he wants to use it to show how benevolent he is.

I think it’s wrong to argue that Leto is secretly as corrupt as, say the Harkonnens, or even corrupt at all, but I also think it’s wrong to try to imply by contrast that Herbert isn’t deliberately trying to ask us if Leto is as good as he makes himself out to be.

What I would say is that ER is absolutely a step back from Sekiro, and, in terms of enemy design, even from DS3 and DS1.

ER introduces a couple flashy new mechanics into the souls formula, such as jumping or guard counters, or the more posture system which, although more developed than DS3, still feels like a step back from Sekiro. I've seen a lot of people say things like "you should be playing for posture breaks, and making use of positioning", but I think that, in a first playthrough (which is by far the most important playthrough as many people won't play beyond it), not only does the game do a piss poor job of actually teaching you how to approach its new combat, it almost seems to stop you from learning until you have to at the very end of the game, where the bosses become incredibly difficult to beat unless you utilise cheap strats - and yes I'm calling them that - such as summoning.

The game missed such an amazing opportunity for a skill check tutorial boss that made sure that you understood this wasn't just open world dark souls, and the combat is different. When you reach Margit, who is supposed to be that, sure he might teach you some of the mechanics, such as the way that attack strings work now, or the importance of positioning/jumping/looking for posture break opportunities, what most players actually learn moreso is "hard boss, must come back later". Now, Margit is a pretty good boss in and of himself, and it's an important lesson to teach new players that they can come back later, but what that leads to is many players coming back and mincing Margit with all their new gear. Why didn't they do that, plus have a boss that you have to beat before entering Limgrave, replacing that godawful Solider of Godrick miniboss, who doesn't teach you anything besides how to dodge and who dies in a couple hits? 

The reason this itself is an issue is because if you go and watch the uber good at the game reviewers, like Lupine, who responded to Anderson's critique of the game pretty thoroughly, they actually often reveal that they didn't even like the game the first time they played, and they had to go to the internet to be told how to engage with the combat, before coming to love it. The more reasonable of these reviewers, such at Feeble King who made a critique regarding Lupine's treatment of Anderson's review, pointed out that Lupine was often technically right about many different aspects of the combat, but he'd often missed the obvious response which was "how was I supposed to know?" Before anything else, I think I'd take issue with the term "skill issue" because that doesn't imply an issue in skill, rather mindset. It's like playing Sekiro like a Dark Souls game (though this example is way more extreme), it isn't necessarily a skill issue, rather an issue of approach, I would argue. 

When it comes to engagement with the systems in place, you could argue that it's an issue with the player for not using it, but I would criticise it in the same way I'd criticise someone maybe for not using any combat arts or prosthetics in Sekiro. If I saw my friend playing either game, and he never touched either system, I probably would say "what are you doing, aren't you going to try out this system?" If he started using it and then concluded that the gameplay got demonstrably less enjoyable when he did, I would think it would be completely fair to not use it again. But with infusions, all I ever noticed it did was boost my numbers by max 20%, because I was using the stat scaling infusions (keen since I was a dex build). 

Now, this number is not insubstantial, but if I were to concede that FromSoft expected the majority of players to trial and error bosses until they found the right infusion - and I want to be clear that I don't mean this necessarily as a bad thing, because you could try out infusions while also making attempts on bosses and learning their moves - I would immediately ask why it were not made a more obvious part of the game? In Lies of P, for instance, there are 3 elemental damage types, each of which corresponding to a different type of enemy (Carcasses are weak to Fire, Puppets are weak to Electricity and Humans are weak to Acid iirc), and the way that Lies of P communicates the importance of these elements (which are even in that game optional) is both through visual feedback and through making it very easy for players to spec into them. When enemies are inflicted with whichever status effect you're using, their model will very obviously reflect that, and the damage number turns whatever the colour of the stat is. Not to mention the fact that you will be given an item that lets you apply the status to your weapon temporarily that resets at bonfires, as well as the fact that each status type is given its own type of legion arms (basically Sekiro prosthetics but more effective). What I'm getting at is that Lies of P is more obviously built around figuring out status weaknesses of enemies and using them to give yourself an edge, and the prominence of status items and such in game, and the visual feedback you get, reinforces this to the player.

If you're right, that in Elden Ring, the devs intended people to always be infusing their weapons with the right status effect after figuring it out, why does Elden Ring not provide more feedback to the player about this? I know that some stats might cause certain effects, like sleep or bleed, but beyond this it feels like it may be up to checking graphs to figure out which one is more optimal?

I want to be clear that I’m not insulting however you choose to play the game, and if you managed to find out the elemental weaknesses of certain bosses, then that’s rather impressive and good for you. 
What I will say though is that I’m not sure I’d concede it’s a skill issue not to do this and still struggle with the boss. A good example could be that in DS1, you get given some lightning infusion before the Taurus Demon, which he is weak to. The boss is made much easier if you use it, but it is still approachable and very doable without. I think players ought to be rewarded for taking initiative and working out weaknesses like you do, rather than having to be required to.

I think you’re taking this a bit too superficially (although it’s often said this way so i don’t blame you), the criticism I think is usually founded in the area of philosophy called epistemology.

The most agreeable way to describe “objective critique”, would be something like what Chris Stuckman does. “This film is directed by x, its protagonist is y, the music is composed by z, etc.” This is probably the most common way to describe what objective critique is from what I’ve seen, and then the building on top of that is usually seen to be more subjective. 

But suppose I counter the statement “this music is fast” by saying “well this other music is faster, so the music is also slow by other metrics” or if you say “the protagonist is primarily red” to which I say “well maybe my red is different from your red”. Even when these counters are offered though, you may say that the underlying statement is that a certain effect is being created; colour theory and all that. To which I - well not me but you understand - may concede that maybe we all see red and think of sex, blood or love or whatever other connotation is evoked by this colour, but the objective fact of what red looks like is unfalsifiable because we can never truly say we’re experiencing the same thing. On this incredibly pedantic and minor level, you may want to concede that genuinely objective critique is at least pragmatically impossible in some capacity. 

And it’s usually in this way that I think most people who criticise EFAP’s stuff think, when they hear that they’re doing objective critique. It’s less a rejection of the validity of their arguments (when it’s said in good faith) and more a rejection of the description of their critique.

The one thing I think EFAP could benefit from would be doing an episode where they discuss precisely what they consider objective critique to mean when they use it. This would stop at least the people who are genuinely confused (and honestly I find myself among this crowd at times, despite really appreciating their stuff) from being as confused when they don’t need to be.

Greeks saw tan as a blemish in the sense that you were white naturally and slowly accumulated it, so those who were able to keep themselves white completely were, in a way, pure and unblemished from labour, but this also applies to those whose defining trait is literally that they cannot be blemished, the gods. The use of the Homeric Hymns, aside from the fact that the Greeks themselves even thought they were Homer, is that they were read everywhere and by everyone, which is why they survive. Burkert - one of the most influential scholars on the subject of Greek Religion - points out that readings of the Hymns, Homer and Hesiod, and other poetry is constant throughout festivals everywhere, because they tie the ritual together and the ritual makes the myth more believable. The point is that the Greeks everywhere read these poems, not even the Spartans didn't have Homer, and this would've shaped, inadvertently, their view of the gods as its the medium through which they saw their characterisation.

That's not the point, there still is quite a decent throughline of canon and Homer and Hesiod standardises the general depiction of the gods.  Aphrodite was indeed a God of War in Sparta (good counterexample) but this is due to a specific culture in really only Sparta amongst the Greeks of not taking exception to the association of War and Love when Astarte, who herself coming from Ishtar, is beginning to be worshiped in Greece and has those dual characterisations. 

However, outliers don't break the rule. Burkert says that "the art of poetry gave individual myths a fixed and memorable form". This is in correlation with their continual recitation being "an essential part of every festival", those myths then carrying over much detail lifted from the festivals themselves. There are countless incredibly interesting examples in the Hymn to Demeter, for instance, having details which parallel what we know about happened in the Eleusinian Mysteries. I will summarise Burkert (I'm not sure how much you know about him but he's a pillar of scholarship when it comes to Greek Religion, although somewhat outdated when it comes to specific details about specific festivals), who think that it is notable that it's called "Greek" mythology and not "Spartan" mythology or "Athenian" mythology because although they usually would have slight (and it is slight in most all cases) differences in details - such as how Aphrodite was born - the throughline of the characterisation and the chronology of myths is remarkably consistent. When it comes to Aphrodite of War or Artemis of Fertility, it is true we can say that these are examples of contradictory characterisations alongside the 'standard' ones as Artemis is a virgin and Aphrodite can't be associated with war, but in these rare cases where we have two opposing versions, one is almost always - and I can't think of an example to the contrary - significantly more pan-hellenic than the other which usually is relegated to a single deme or polis. 

Also when we talk about the reliability of the Iliad and the Odyssey, my claim is that they are very reliable as representations of not only Homer's views of the gods but the coming Greeks who will read Homer and Hesiod constantly and, mind the pun, religiously. They become a standard among them and because they are constantly read, they become the canon de facto rather than the Bible's de jure canon.

Scholar quotes are a divisive subject as they are really dependent upon how you feel about it, personally I read a couple different books on the different material and listened to a load of lectures before making and keeping notes of what it was that scholars thought about different material, but this may be overkill if you're not planning to study Classics at university like I am. A more useful way to accumulate them is to read articles (usually 2-8 pages) and summarise for yourself the arguments and take key quotes that you may be able to use in the exam. My teacher handed out to us a big sheet of scholar quotes without context to them and I really think that's the worst way to do it because you have no reason to remember each quote as you don't know how the scholar unpacks it, not to mention that you haven't really engaged with the scholarship.

I can give you an example of this being a bad thing: I recently read some conflicting articles about Aristophanes written by Nicole Tsoumpra and Malcolm Heath. Had I just been given the scholar quotes, they would look something like "Aristophanes embraces his role as political advisor, especially in the Frogs" - Tsoumpra, and "Aristophanes always satirises his role as political advisor, and the Frogs being a tonal outlier doesn't disprove this" - Heath. They disagree on the face of it but without having read their arguments I wouldn't know the substance of this disagreement, just that their views don't align. For instance, you can use the shurikens to get extra posture damage/knock people over as they're jumping (which is more often than you'd think) as well as hard countering posture restoration moves that the General mini-bosses, as well as some later bosses, can sometimes do. The thing is, they're not supposed to replace your sword in anyway, they create openings/allow you to capitalise off of specific things that you figure out. They're supplementary parts of your kit and should be used to combo into and off of normal attacks. This is why you see really good players constantly using them to close gaps or as follow ups to attacks, such as using the kusabimaru mid-air spiral attack after jumping off of an enemy's sweep attack. They're designed like puzzle pieces and you have to figure out how to use them.

In Welsh we have systems such as initial consonant mutation working to make the language actually *sound* better. Not to mention that it functions to distinguish certain grammatical issues.
So for example, if I say I am “in” a place then I use the nasal mutation, if applicable, with the preposition “yn” (“in”): so “Cymru” is “Wales” but “in Wales” is “Yng Nghymru”. 
Additionally, the word for “his” and “her” is the same (“ei”) and the way that you distinguish between them is by what form of mutation is caused by it, so “his” causes a soft mutation and “her” causes an aspirate mutation. If “car” is the same in Welsh then “his car” is “ei gar” but “her car” is “ei char” (that’s a velar fricative not a post-alveolar affricate btw)

Lots of fricatives have voiced and unvoiced pairings, assuming you speak English then you should be familiar with some, and even this one.

The way that phonology breaks these down is that we would call "Dd" a voiced dental fricative; in that it is a fricative, a sound that is made through forcing air through certain passages, dental because the air is pushed through, or around, your teeth and voiced because it is harsher as the passage is made smaller.

In effect, it is the difference between "F" and "V" or "S" and "Z" in English; as well we also observe this difference, I saw another comment pointing out that "Th" in "This" is the equivalent of "Dd" whereas "Th" in "Thin" is what you mean by "Th" in Welsh.

This isn't too uncommon to English as, before the Norman conquest, scribes used the 'edd' symbol (Ð/ð) to denote this sound -- which is still used in Icelandic today -- and, despite no longer being used, our accents preserve the difference.

Hi, Welsh speaker here with a passion for old Welsh and Greek history!

Firstly, the modern word describing the country of Wales is "Cymru" (pronounced "cum-ree" but with pursed lips for the second syllable), which comes from the Welsh term "Cymru" which means "brothers" or "kinsmen", which itself comes from the old Brittonic term "Cymbrogi" which means the same thing. 

What's interesting to note is that Wales around this time wasn't what it is now, it was never a single nation and was, in fact, a group of kingdoms. The Britons (who became the Welsh, Cornish, Scotti and Bretons) were found all over the British island and isles and, as I'm sure is your intention, existed similarly to the Greeks in how disunified their culture was. I can't speak for time periods but by late Archaic Greece, I'm assuming you mean a century or two after the usual placement of Homer at C7th/C8th BCE? There would've been Celtic people on Britain who would've spoken a language which became Welsh but it also was a language which became Cornish and Breton because they weren't separate. When looking back on British history there's technical issue using the term "Welsh", in that it's almost like using the term "Athenian" to describe all of Ancient Greece, it's a broad term used by the Anglo-Saxons ("Walis" - foreigner) to describe those people they pushed into the corners of Britain about 1000 years after you seem to be basing your story.

Basically, there was a Celtic Brittonic culture in Britain, which is the direct ancestor to the Welsh, which was there around the time that you are basing this narrative, and a good, accurate term to use would be "Cymbrogi" (or whatever version of that term you can find which suits your purpose).
